chapter_title: Concerning the Cross of Light: [...] trample upon

14.content: they will be able to diss

spiritual_reading:
When you are led by obedience to serve what is holy, and you apply your life to it, no evil is imputed to you. For then your effort is not driven by craving, nor by the love of self‑advantage where sin is; but your activity is ordered by what is Divine, and your urgency is from use and not from your proprium.

Truly, I declare openly: every person who has been made receptive of good and truth, and who advances in life for the sake of Divine use, even while he is in the natural degree and acting in its lowest things, does not thereby bring guilt upon himself. Rather, his whole progress is crowned with blessedness and victory, because he is not moved by self‑will, nor carried by eagerness for possession and vanity while he is in externals.

But the one who presses forward from his own craving and from the lusts of his natural life, and turns his powers toward possession and empty ends, makes his whole course evil; for he advances in falsity and deviation, and his life is a pathway of sin.

See, then: if one is sent by a genuine guide into the performance of a holy use, the whole endeavor is victory. Yet you say within yourself that in doing external acts you seem to profane what is holy and to do violence to it, and you fear that the deed carries guilt.

Do not fear even this, for the living mind is such that it is sometimes troubled in its lower powers while it is being restored. As when disorder seizes the faculties of a person, and his love grows weak, and his interior life is distressed, and he feels pain from that disorder, he seeks one who has knowledge to restore him and to strengthen what rules within him. And the one who heals attends to him and returns him to soundness from the evil that had risen up against him; and the sufferer understands this.

So also there comes one who is wise in the methods of genuine restoration. When he sets himself to remove the evil in the one entrusted to him, he applies the truths he knows, and he even presses hard upon the person’s disordered powers. Yet the one who is being healed recognizes that this severe dealing is for the sake of cure, not from any prior hostility. Everything done is done that the natural life may be restored to right order. Thus the evil and the pain are driven out by means that feel like oppression, because benefit is being brought about. Therefore the one who is being healed cannot rightly hold hatred against the one who disciplines and presses upon his states, since he knows the action is for his good.

But if one were to assault his states from hostility, he would rightly resist and refuse; for he would perceive that the pressure is from enmity, and that what is done from reckless impulse adds further evil to the evil already present.

Therefore the speech that truly harms is this: when someone lets thought and intention go forth in order to destroy what is living, whether in another person, or in lower affections, or in perceptions of truth, and even to violate what is holy; when speech proceeds as falsity, as anger, as bitterness, as envy and malice, or as an accusation spread against a companion—this is the utterance that wounds. If a person brings it forth, it is fittingly sin, because he has opened a way for hellish influences to act through it; and he fastens himself by it to the evil he has chosen. For anyone who binds his inner life to such intention binds himself; and when his outward life is laid aside, he is held in the state in which he had held himself.

It is like this with one who restores wisely: when a harmful falsity has become embedded in the natural life like a deep injury, he acts from understanding and removes what corrupts. He exposes what is hidden, separates it, and applies truths that can dissolve what has hardened. He may also use severe discernment that feels sharp, casting out what is poisonous by means that penetrate, until the fever of disorder is cleansed away. Afterward he applies gentler truths that comfort and conjoin, and the injured state is healed. The one being restored may feel the severity, yet he does not form resentment against the one who corrects him, because he understands that it is being done for his benefit and recovery. Indeed, after the hard reproof and the burning removal of evil, he gives gratitude to the one who healed him, and remains in friendship with him thereafter.

fills.notes: The spiritual sense specifies self-advantage as the spring of sin; the oldest-layer register expresses this as the acquisitive love (gain) rather than a moralizing term.
Required by the opposition in the sentence: haste from use, not from self-desire.
The other path is driven by bodily craving in the natural degree; the substrate contrasts holy use vs. lusts.
He 'turns' or 'sets' his powers toward acquisition; this matches the spiritual sense: turning his powers toward possession.
Pairs with 'acquisition' as vanity and empty ends in the spiritual sense.
The clause needs a summative adverb before the conclusion 'a total sin is the walkway'; corresponds to the idea that the whole course is evil.
Introduces the recap and application ('behold, I have told you'), matching the spiritual 'See, then'.
The healer acts on 'the one entrusted to him' in the spiritual sense; in the natural image this is the patient committed to the doctor’s care.
In the spiritual sense the harmful utterance includes envy and malice; in this register 'envy and hatred' is the common pair.
What is wounded by such speech, in this oldest cosmological layer, is the living soul bound in created forms (persons, animals, trees, Cross of Light).
The spiritual sense says he opens a way for hellish influences; the substrate idiom is 'demons and powers of Darkness' acting through the utterance.
Refers back to the uttered saying as the channel by which demons are brought forth to act.
Directly corresponds to 'he fastens himself by it to the evil he has chosen' and anticipates 'bind him in the place'.
The logic requires an infinitival purpose: he binds his word to the fetter so that he may bind himself; the repeated binding motif governs the whole passage.
Parallelism: 'anyone who would bind his word to the fetter'—the act itself is the binding.
Concludes the maxim: whoever binds his word (inner intention in speech) binds himself.
The final clause requires what is bound: when he comes forth (leaves the body), he is bound where he had bound his soul, i.e., his ruling love/state.
The doctor-image corresponds to removing embedded disorder; 'turn back the evil within' matches the spiritual 'harmful falsity embedded'.
He 'cuts open' to expose what is hidden, matching the spiritual: exposes what is hidden, separates it.
The doctor both cuts and heals; required to keep the sequence: incision, removal, purification, then healing.
Corresponds to exposing what is hidden before separating and removing it.
Matches the extraction motif: casts out what is poisonous.

fills.fill: they will be able to diss

fills.notes: After purification, the soothing drugs are applied 'upon it' (the wound) before it heals up.
The restored one gives thanks (and then rewards) to the doctor; matches the spiritual 'gives gratitude'.
Keeps the antithesis: he gives thanks and rewards, but does not hate or resent.

assessment: Most gaps are tightly constrained by the correspondential structure: the chapter opposes motion from obedience and holy use vs. motion from lust and gain; and it develops the healer image to justify severe external pressure that serves internal restoration. The hardest restorations are places where the Coptic Vorlage likely had idiomatic connectors (¶5 #4; ¶14 #4) and the long binding sequence in ¶12, but even there the spiritual logic of intention becoming a fetter strongly constrains the required vocabulary (bind, fetter, soul, powers of Darkness).
